<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: Supervision (HUMPS) Act,'' Fitzgerald) above in the
section on poison pills.
• Sec. 302: H.R. 940--the ``Fair Audits and
Inspection for Regulators'' Exams (FAIR Exams) Act''
(Hill), (5/21/25 markup, 35-17). This section would
impose certain timelines for examiners from the Federal
Reserve, FDIC, OCC, NCUA, and CFPB to share exam
reports, as well as all supporting documentation, with
a financial institution they supervise following an
exam. This bill would also establish an Office of
Independent Examination Review (OIER) within the FFIER
to review appeals of material supervisory
determinations (MSD) issued by these Federal agencies
for financial institutions they supervise, including
the largest banks, which would further be subject to
judicial review. GAO and other experts said the problem
with Silicon Valley Bank was not due process, but
rather, that supervisory concerns were not elevated
quickly enough to ensure they were addressed. The
Committee found similar dynamics at Wells Fargo, as the
bank received various citations that snowballed into
significant and repeated consumer harm. Accordingly,
this bill would significantly weaken the supervisory
framework and undermine consumer protection as well as
the safety and soundness of depository institutions.
While the ANS makes some changes to this section, Fed staff have indicated that this section would make it more difficult to bring routine supervisory actions and could result in significant delays before the Fed could require an institution to address a serious safety and soundness concern, which would adversely impact the effectiveness of their enforcement program. This approach is the exact opposite of what is needed following the SVB failure, where the Fed's slow supervisory and enforcement approach was heavily criticized for contributing to SVB's failure.
• Sec. 303: H.R. 4437--the ``Supervisory
Modification for Appropriate Risk-Based Testing (SMART)
Act'' (Timmons), (7/22/25 markup, 53-1). This section
provides exam relief for well-managed and well-
capitalized banks and credit unions with under $6
billion in total assets, provided they are not subject
to an enforcement action or recently went through a
merger. Specifically, the bill provides these
institutions with alternating full-scope and limited-
scope exam as well as a combined exam (safety and
soundness; consumer compliance; and/or cybersecurity
and information technology), however regulators retain
discretion to do additional targeted or full-scope
exams to ensure safety and soundness and compliance
with applicable laws.
• Sec. 304: H.R. 4478--the ``Tailored
Regulatory Updates for Supervisory Testing (TRUST)
Act'' (Moore-NC), (7/23/25 markup, 48-0). This section
raises the consolidated asset threshold from $3 billion
to $6 billion for well-capitalized and well-managed
banks (including not being subject to an enforcement
action) to qualify for an 18-month full-scope
examination cycle instead of a 12-month exam. Congress
last raised this threshold in 2018, when this threshold
covered 94.2% of banks. After first proposing to raise
this threshold to $10 billion, Republicans agreed to
lower this to a $6 billion threshold, which would cover
94.6% of banks today.
• Sec. 305: H.R. 2702--the ``Financial
Integrity and Regulation Management (FIRM) Act''
(Barr), (5/21/25 markup, 33-19). Instead of focusing on
debanking resulting in closed or frozen accounts, this
section would completely eliminate reputational risk as
a component of the supervision of depository
institutions. For the first time, regulators would be
prevented from considering certain types of risk, in
this case reputational risk, when promoting safety and
soundness. Republicans adopted an amendment offered by
Rep. Sherman to exempt reputational risk concerns
related to terrorist financing, however there remain
many other types of issues, including repeat offenders
and other instances of money laundering, that could be
tougher to curb based on this section. Title IV--Regulatory Accountability and Transparency
• See description of Section 401 (H.R. 3446,
the ``FDIC Board Accountability Act,'' Huizenga),
Section 402 (H.R. 4460, the ``Stop Agency Fiat
Enforcement of Guidance (SAFE Guidance) Act,'' Meuser),
Section 403 (H.R. 6544, the ``Regulatory Efficiency,
Verification, Itemization, and Enhanced Workflow
(REVIEW) Act,'' Timmons), and Section 404 (H.R. 6550,
the ``American Financial Institution Regulatory
Sovereignty and Transparency (American FIRST) Act,''
Loudermilk) above in the section on poison pills. Title V--Strengthening Local Bank Funding
• Sec. 501: H.R. 3390--the ``Bringing the
Discount Window into the 21st Century Act'' (De La
Cruz), (7/23/25 markup, 48-1). This section would
require the Federal Reserve to conduct a review,
develop a plan, and issue reports on steps they are
taking to enhance and modernize the functioning of the
Fed's discount window where banks obtain emergency
liquidity. This is in response to concerns raised by
banks that had problems accessing the Fed's discount
window during the 2023 regional bank failures.
• Sec. 502: H.R. 3234--the ``Keeping Deposits
Local Act'' (Emmer), (9/16/25 markup, 51-0). This
section would modify limits first set by Congress in
2018 to increase the amount of reciprocal deposits
exempted from brokered deposit restrictions, utilizing
a tiered approach based on a bank's total assets and
total liabilities. Reciprocal deposits are part of a
network operated by a third-party where a bank, for a
fee, may provide insurance for a customer on funds
greater than $250,000. Funds over the cap are
distributed to other banks in the network, and those
banks reciprocate and provide the originating bank
matching funds so it may use the full amount of the
deposit for lending or other purposes. A bipartisan
amendment was adopted to narrow the scope to ensure
community and mid-size banks benefit the most.
• Sec. 503: H.R. 5317--the ``Community Bank
Deposit Access Act'' (Hill), (9/16/25 markup, 48-2).
This provision would allow banks to maintain custodial
deposits and have them exempted from brokered deposit
restrictions. Custodial deposits allow smaller banks to
ensure a customer with more than $250,000 in deposits
can obtain FDIC insurance for the full amount of their
deposit, spreading the funds across other banks in a
custodial deposit network. A bipartisan amendment was
agreed to that narrowed the bill to ensure it focuses
on community banks with less than $10 billion. Title VI--Promoting Bank Competition and Merger Clarity
• See description of Section 601 (H.R. 5262,
the ``Bank Competition Modernization Act,'' Fitzgerald)
above in the section on poison pills.
• Sec. 602: H.R. 6570--the ``Merger Agreement
Approvals Clarity and Predictability Act''
(Fitzgerald), (12/17/25 markup, 52-0). This section
requires GAO to study the use of commitments and
conditions by Federal prudential regulators in
connection with bank merger applications, as well as
other aspects of bank merger reviews and the impact
mergers have had on affected communities, competition,
and financial stability.
• Sec. 603: H.R. 6546--the ``Merger Process
Review Act'' (Williams), (12/17/25 markup, 52-0). This
section requires the Inspectors General of Federal
banking regulators to every three years review the
regulator's handling of bank merger applications,
including the impact bank mergers have had on affected
communities, competition, and financial stability. It
also requires the regulators to respond to the IG
reports with a written plan on how they will improve
the bank merger review process.
• See description of Section 604 (H.R. 1900,
the ``Bank Failure Prevention Act,'' Barr) above in the
section on poison pills.
Title VII--Strengthening Transparency and Involvement in Bank
Resolutions
• Sec. 701: H.R. 6547--the ``Least Cost
Exception Act'' (Flood), (12/17/25 markup, 50-0). This
section would allow the FDIC to waive the least cost
resolution test when selecting a bid for a failed bank
if the FDIC and Federal Reserve make a determination
that any risks to the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund are
outweighed by limiting the concentration in Global
Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) if the FDIC
chooses a bid from a bank other than a G-SIB. The
alternative bid will need to meet certain criteria,
including agreeing to pay the difference of their bid
and that of a G-SIB, subject to case-by-case discounts
and other criteria established by the FDIC.
• Sec. 702: H.R. 6555--the ``Enhancing Bank
Resolution Participation Act'' (Huizenga), (12/17/25
markup, 51-0). This section requires a study by Federal
banking regulators on the use of so-called ``shelf
charters'' and modified bidder qualifications since
2008 to allow nonbank companies to buy a failing bank.
Republicans agreed to expand the study to also consider
safety and soundness, the availability of financial
products and services provided to consumers, and the
risks and benefits of private equity's involvement in
such acquisitions.
• Sec. 703: H.R. 6556, the ``Failing Bank
Acquisition Fairness Act'' (Lynch), (12/17/25 markup,
51-0). This section was added by the ANS and previously
passed the House with broad support when it was
included in Housing for 21st Century. This section
would promote competition in banking by narrowing the
exception that allows a megabank with more than 10% of
U.S. total deposits or liabilities to bid to acquire a
failing bank. Specifically, this bill would prevent
such megabanks from bidding for a failed bank if there
are other eligible bids from other well-capitalized and
well-managed banks that meet FDIC's typical
requirements. Only when there are no such bids would
these megabanks be permitted to acquire a failing bank.
• Sec. 704: H.R. 3716, the ``Systemic Risk
Authority Transparency Act'' (Green), (6/10/26 markup,
51-0). This section was added by the ANS and previously
passed the House with broad support when it was
included in Housing for 21st Century. This section
would require GAO and bank regulators to issue reports
if regulators invoke the systemic risk exception, as
they did to manage the failures of Silicon Valley Bank
and Signature Bank in 2023. These reports would provide
Congress and the public an analysis to identify the
causes of the bank failures, including any management,
supervisory, or regulatory shortcomings.
Title VIII--Facilitating Innovation and Bank Partnerships
• Sec. 801: H.R. 5291--the ``Merchant Banking
Modernization Act'' (Williams), (9/16/25 markup, 35-
17). This section would permit financial holding
companies (FHCs), a type of bank holding company, to
hold merchant banking investments for up to 15 years.
The Fed's regulations currently set a limit of 10 years
on these investments, though they may grant individual
extensions based on the circumstance and could modify
the regulation. Most of these investments are done by
the largest banks, and allow the bank to make engage in
non-financial business activities that may pose unusual
risks. Without more data about these kind of unique
investments, such a reform could undermine the safety
and soundness of large banks operating in this space.
• Sec. 802: H.R. 6552--the ``Bank FinTech
Partnership Enhancement Act'' (Barr), (12/17/25 markup,
53-0). This section requires the Federal banking and
credit union regulators to conduct a study of how
fintech partnerships could help banks and credit unions
better compete and serve their communities. Republicans
added considerations for consumer protection as well as
availability of financial products and services for
consumers.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
